explain.say: In late summer 1854 cholera killed hundreds of people in a few streets of Soho, London, within days. Most doctors blamed bad air, called miasma. A doctor named John Snow did something new. Watch the chain. He marked each death on a map, and saw them crowd around one water pump on Broad Street. What would you do next?

explain.say: Snow had the pump handle removed on 8 September, and argued cholera spread through dirty water. Look at the timeline. In the following decades Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch proved that microbes cause disease, germ theory, and cities built sewers and clean water supplies. Which came first, the cure or the clean water?

explain.say: Here are real numbers, approximately. World life expectancy was about 29 years in 1800 and 32 in 1900, then leapt to about 46 by 1950 and about 73 by 2019. In the UK it went from about 40 in 1850 to about 81. Much of the early gain came from fewer babies and children dying. Which line rises faster after 1950?

Why did people start living longer? See the debate. Thomas McKeown argued better food mattered most, since deaths fell before effective drugs. Simon Szreter replied that public health, clean water, sewers and city government, did most. Antibiotics and vaccines then added huge gains. Which side do you lean to?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Food, water and medicine each played a part.

explain.say: Look at the map for a triumph. The World Health Organization, based in Geneva, led a campaign that tracked smallpox village by village, including a huge effort in India. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 smallpox was declared eradicated, the first disease ever wiped out. Wonderful work. Challenge: which disease might be next?

faq.q: How did John Snow stop cholera?
faq.a: During the 1854 Soho outbreak, Snow mapped the deaths and found they clustered around the Broad Street water pump. He persuaded officials to remove the pump handle on 8 September 1854 and argued that cholera spreads through contaminated water, not bad air.
asks: What was the Broad Street pump?

faq.a: The idea, proved by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch from the 1860s to the 1880s, that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. It replaced miasma theory and led to antiseptic surgery, vaccines and modern hygiene.

faq.q: Why did life expectancy rise so much?
faq.a: Fewer infants and children died, thanks to better nutrition, clean water and sewers, housing, vaccines, antibiotics and medical care. Thomas McKeown stressed nutrition; Simon Szreter stressed public health action. World life expectancy rose from about 32 in 1900 to about 73 in 2019.

From 1967 the WHO intensified a global campaign using surveillance and ring vaccination: finding each case and vaccinating everyone around it. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated in May 1980.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould killed bacteria. Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team turned it into a usable drug around 1940, and it was mass-produced during the Second World War.

facts: John Snow had the Broad Street pump handle removed on 8 September 1854.
The World Health Organization was founded in 1948.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in May 1980.

quiz.why: The cluster around the Broad Street pump pointed to contaminated water.
